title: The Elephant in Rut
summary: Having wrenched the firm post of evaṃkāra and broken bonds of many kinds, Kāṇha plays, drunk on liquor, and enters the lotus grove of the innate. The more the elephant lusts for the she-elephant, the more the ichor of suchness rains down; all six realms are pure by nature, and the poet, seizing the jewel of the ten powers, tames the elephant of knowledge. Munidatta reads the elephant as the mind and as Kāṇha himself, whose union with the goddess Nairātmā rains the ichor of suchness (cp.09.m1, cp.09.m3), and the elephant of the last line as ignorance (cp.09.m5).

lines.gloss: rāga (melody) · Paṭamañjarī · (of Kāhnupāda: the attribution written before the song)

flags.note: The poet's name is not in রাগ পটমঞ্জরী itself. It comes from the attribution kāhnupādānām, 'of Kāhnupāda', which Shastri's text writes before the song and which the input removes from line 1a as no part of the verse; the Tibetan heading also names the poet (nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyi'o). If the heading should render only the rāga, drop '· Kāṇha'.

lines.gloss: evaṃkāra (the syllables e-vaṃ) · firm · post · having-twisted/wrenched

flags.note: Construction. I take evaṃkāra together with 'the firm post' (dṛṛha bākhoṛa): the post that is wrenched is the evaṃkāra, or belongs to it. This keeps the Bengali word order and suits Munidatta, who makes e and vaṃ a pair and sets it beside 'vākhoṛa, the pair of pillars', which is crushed (cp.09.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'e waM yi ge brtan byas ka gnyis nyed', 'having made the letters e vaṃ firm, (he) crushes the two pillars', supplying a verb for dṛṛha and keeping the evaṃkāra apart from the pillars. Alternative: 'Making the evaṃkāra firm, wrenching the post'.

bākhoṛa is 'post' in the glossary, but Munidatta (stambhadvaya, cp.09.m2) and the Tibetan (ka gnyis) both have a pair of pillars. moḍḍiu: 'twisting, wrenching' (compare Bengali moṛā, 'to twist'); 'crushing' is possible, with Munidatta's marddayitvā and the Tibetan nyed.

lines.gloss: various · pervading · bond(s) · having-broken · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: breaking the pervading [bonds]{bandhana} of many kinds,

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends the line with ston, 'shows, teaches' ('rnam pa sna tshogs khyab byed 'ching ba ston'), where the Bengali has toṛiu, 'having broken'. Probably a slip in the Tibetan: its comment speaks of removing the obstruction ('gog pa phyung nas).
viāpaka (vyāpaka), 'pervading': the line does not say what the bonds pervade; Munidatta says the avadhūtī (cp.09.m2). 'Pervasive' would also do.

lines.gloss: innate · lotus-grove · having-entered · at-peace(?) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: he enters the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} of the [innate]{sahaja} and is at peace.

flags.note: nibitā is uncertain. I take it as Sanskrit nirvṛta, 'at peace, content, at rest'; nivṛtta, 'ceased, withdrawn', is possible. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems med gyur, 'became without mind (or thought)', and Munidatta's paraphrase ends 'plays in a form free of concepts' (nirvikalpākāre, cp.09.m2).

lines.en: The more the [elephant]{elephant} lusts for the [she-elephant]{karini},

flags.note: jima jima ... tima tima (yathā yathā ... tathā tathā): 'the more ... the more', the usual sense of the doubled correlative, or 'just as ... so', a simple comparison, as in Munidatta's paraphrase (yathā ... tadvat, cp.09.m3). I chose the first.

risaa: probably from Sanskrit īrṣyati, 'is jealous, is passionate (for)'; Munidatta has īrṣyāmada, 'the ichor of jealous passion' (cp.09.m3), and the Tibetan chags, 'is attached, lusts'. 'Lusts for' is my compromise.

lines.translit: tima tima tathatā maa gala varisaa || dhru ||
lines.gloss: so · so · suchness · ichor · cheek(?) · rains · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: the more the [ichor]{mada} of [suchness]{tathata} rains down his cheeks.

flags.note: gala: 'cheek' (compare Bengali gāl; the Tibetan has ngos 'gram, 'side of the cheek'), or from galati, 'drips' ('suchness rains, dripping ichor'). tathatā could also be the subject ('suchness rains ichor'); Munidatta's tathatāmada, 'ichor of suchness' (cp.09.m3), supports my reading. 'His' is supplied by the English.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), 'de lta de ltar de nyid ngos 'gram 'bab', has no word for the ichor (maa): 'just so, suchness flows down the cheek'.

lines.en: All the [six realms]{sadgati} are pure by [nature]{svabhava};

lines.gloss: being-and-nonbeing · hair-tip · not · impure(?) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: in [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, not a hair's tip is impure.

flags.note: chudha is unclear. Following Munidatta, 'not even a hair's tip that is impure exists' (cp.09.m4), I take na chudha as 'is not impure', continuing 4a. If chudha is śuddha, 'pure' (like sūdha in 4a), the line says the opposite: 'not a hair's tip is pure'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'dngos dang dngos med la chags ma dag pa', 'attachment to things and non-things is impure', apparently hearing lāga, 'attached', in balāga rather than vālāgra, 'hair's tip', and taking na chudha as 'not pure'. This puts the sense of the line in doubt.

lines.en: Seizing the [jewel]{ratna} of the [ten powers]{dasabala} in the [ten directions]{dasadis},

flags.note: haria: 'having seized, taken' (Sanskrit hṛta), as Munidatta's hāritam, 'taken' (cp.09.m5); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'phro, 'radiates' ('the jewel of the ten powers radiates into the ten directions'). Whether 'in the ten directions' goes with the jewel or with the seizing is also open.

lines.gloss: knowledge-elephant · I-tame(?) · without-affliction/without-trouble · (refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: vidyākari, 'elephant of knowledge', is what the Bengali and the Tibetan song (rig pa'i glang dbang) read. Munidatta (cp.09.m5) and the Tibetan comment read avidyā: 'the lord-elephant of ignorance'. I have not harmonized them; the reviewer should decide.

damakum̐ looks like a first-person present, 'I tame' (compare Apabhraṃśa -aüṃ). Munidatta paraphrases damanaṃ kuru, an imperative, 'tame' (cp.09.m5). The Tibetan song has btsal, 'sought', perhaps a slip for btul, 'tamed'.

akilesem̐ (akleśena): in ordinary Sanskrit 'without trouble, easily'; literally 'without affliction'. I keep the literal sense and mark the glossary term. Munidatta has 'through non-attachment' (anāsaṅgena, cp.09.m5); the Tibetan song, nyon mongs nyid kyis, 'by the afflictions themselves', lacks the negative.

notes.text: [Rāga]{raga}: a melodic mode of Indian music; the heading names the one to which the song is sung, here Paṭamañjarī. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song 'pa Da ha'i tshogs pa zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyi'o', 'the song called Paḍaha'i tshogs pa, of Kṛṣṇācāryapāda', partly transcribing and partly translating the rāga's name (tshogs pa, 'cluster, gathering', perhaps for mañjarī).

Shastri's text writes the attribution kāhnupādānām, 'of Kāhnupāda', before the song; the input removes it from line 1a as no part of the verse. I have put the poet's name in the heading, as the Tibetan heading also does.

Munidatta introduces the song: Kṛṣṇācāryapāda, filled with dense joy, says the same thing in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, picturing it through the word 'mind-elephant' (cittagajendra, the mind as lord of elephants). He thus reads the song's elephant as the mind, and in his comments on couplets 1 and 3 he names Kāṇha himself as that elephant. The Tibetan comment renders the figure of speech (utprekṣā) as gzugs kyi rgyun, perhaps a slip for gzugs kyi rgyan, 'ornament of form'.

Munidatta comments on couplets 1 and 2 together, then calls couplet 3 'another verse', couplet 4 the third and couplet 5 the fourth, leaving the refrain out of the count. Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after couplet 1 as well as after the refrain and the later couplets; it is not translated. The poet names himself in the refrain, not in the last couplet.

[Evaṃkāra]{evamkara}: the syllables e and vaṃ, which open the formula 'Thus (evaṃ) have I heard' at the head of sūtras and tantras; in the yoginī tantras the pair stands for the female and the male, wisdom and means, joined.

Bākhoṛa, 'post, pillar', is a word of uncertain origin; Munidatta renders it stambhadvaya, 'a pair of pillars', and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ka gnyis, 'two pillars', so the singular 'post' may be too narrow. Moḍḍiu is an absolutive, 'having twisted, wrenched' (compare Bengali moṛā, 'to twist'); Munidatta paraphrases marddayitvā, 'having crushed', and the Tibetan song has nyed, 'crush, knead'. The absolutives of couplet 1 (moḍḍiu, toṛiu) have no subject of their own; Munidatta runs them into the refrain, whose subject is Kāṇha.

Read literally, couplet 1 with the refrain gives the picture of a tethered elephant breaking loose: it wrenches the post it is tied to, snaps its fetters and, maddened, plays in a lotus pond. The elephant itself is named only in couplet 3, but mātā in the refrain ('drunk', Sanskrit matta) is the usual word for an elephant maddened in rut.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line 'e waM yi ge brtan byas ka gnyis nyed', 'having made the letters e vaṃ firm, (he) crushes the two pillars': it takes dṛṛha as 'made firm' and keeps the evaṃkāra apart from the pillars. I have taken 'the firm post' and the evaṃkāra together, which is closer to the Bengali word order and to Munidatta, who makes e and vaṃ the pair that is crushed.

Munidatta reads e as the [moon]{moon}-[appearance]{abhasa} and vaṃ as the [sun]{surya}, the two together being 'the knowledge of day and night'; he sets them beside 'vākhoṛa, the pair of pillars', which are crushed and made free of appearance by the process of [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}. The Tibetan comment assigns the syllables the other way round: 'baM yig zla ba'i snang ba e yig nyi ma', 'the syllable vaṃ is the moon-appearance, the syllable e the sun'.

Munidatta takes the [bonds]{bandhana} as the binding of many kinds that pervades the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (the central channel of the subtle body), broken once the moon and sun have been made free of appearance. The Tibetan comment has 'the obstruction pervading the avadhūtī' (a wa d+hU tI khyab byed 'gog pa), removed (phyung nas).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'rnam pa sna tshogs khyab byed 'ching ba ston', 'shows the pervading bonds of many kinds', with ston, 'shows, teaches', where the Bengali has toṛiu, 'having broken'. This may be a copying slip in the Tibetan; its comment on the passage speaks of removing the obstruction ('gog pa phyung nas), which agrees with the Bengali.

Vilasaa, 'plays, sports' (Sanskrit vilasati); āsavamātā, 'drunk on liquor' (āsava + matta). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'kAh+Na rtse zhing sbrang gi chang gis myos', 'Kāṇha plays and is drunk on mead', making the liquor a honey liquor (sbrang gi chang). The refrain carries the poet's self-naming; the song has no other.

Nibitā is uncertain. I take it from Sanskrit nirvṛta, 'at peace, content, at rest'; nivṛtta, 'turned back, ceased', is also possible. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems med gyur, 'became without mind (or thought)', and Munidatta's paraphrase ends 'plays in a form free of concepts' (nirvikalpākāre krīḍanti). Either may reflect a different understanding of the word, or simply a gloss.

Munidatta: Kṛṣṇācārya, 'the lord of elephants that is knowledge' (jñānagajendra), is drunk from drinking the [liquor]{asava} of [non-apprehension]{anupalambha} of 'these three' (not named; perhaps the two appearances and the bonds of couplet 1), and, having made the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} the lotus of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, plays in a form free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}. The Tibetan comment has 'having gone to the lotus grove of great bliss'. He supports this with a verse he attributes to [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna}, which ends with the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, skilled in the drama of illusion, at play (krīḍati), the same verb he uses for Kāṇha.

A bull elephant in rut (musth) exudes a dark fluid, ichor (mada), from glands on its temples, and it runs down the cheeks; in Indian poetry the flowing ichor is the sign of the elephant's passion and fury. Mada also means intoxication, which echoes the drunken Kāṇha of the refrain.

Jima jima ... tima tima (Sanskrit yathā yathā ... tathā tathā) usually means 'the more ... the more'; Munidatta's paraphrase (yathā ... tadvat) and the Tibetan (ji lta ji ltar ... de lta de ltar) can be read as a plain comparison, 'just as ... so'. Risaa is probably from Sanskrit īrṣyati, 'is jealous, is passionate'; Munidatta speaks of the elephant's īrṣyāmada, the ichor of jealous passion, and the Tibetan has chags, 'is attached, lusts'.

Gala is probably 'cheek' (compare Bengali gāl), where an elephant's ichor runs. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees, 'de nyid ngos 'gram 'bab', 'suchness flows down the side of the cheek', but has no word for the ichor (maa). A derivation from Sanskrit galati, 'drips, oozes', is also possible. Munidatta's paraphrase has only 'rain the ichor of suchness' (tathatāmadaṃ pravarṣanti).

Munidatta: with another verse Kāṇha says the same thing. As an outer elephant bears the ichor of jealous passion toward a she-elephant, so the mind-elephant Kṛṣṇācāryapāda, through union with the [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati} Nairātmā ('She who is without self'), rains down the [ichor]{mada} of [suchness]{tathata}. The Tibetan comment has the outer elephant 'run' with the intoxication of desire for the she-elephant, and gives 'the liquor of suchness' (de bzhin nyid kyi chang) for the ichor.

Munidatta: with the third verse Kāṇha speaks of perceiving the [true nature]{svarupa} of things. The six realms are beings born from eggs, from wombs, spontaneously and from moisture, of the nature of gods, asuras and the rest; for the lord of yogis all things are pure by nature, and not even a hair's tip that is impure exists. He quotes a verse from the [Madhyamakaśāstra]{tx-madhyamakasastra}: nothing here is to be removed, nothing added; the real should be seen as real, and whoever sees the real is freed. Where the Sanskrit speaks of perceiving the true nature of things (bhāvānāṃ svarūpopalabdhi), the Tibetan comment has 'the apprehension of things and non-things' (dngos po dang dngos po med pa'i dmigs pa).

Balāga is Sanskrit vālāgra, 'the tip of a hair', as Munidatta's bālāgram shows. Chudha is uncertain. I follow Munidatta's paraphrase, 'not even a hair's tip that is impure exists' (bālāgram apy apariśuddhaṃ kiñcin na vidyate), so that chudha would mean 'impure, stained' (perhaps from Sanskrit kṣubdha, 'stirred, turbid'; a guess). Read as śuddha, 'pure', like sūdha in 4a, the line would say the opposite: 'in being and nonbeing, not a hair's tip is pure'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'dngos dang dngos med la chags ma dag pa', 'attachment to things and non-things is impure': it seems to hear lāga, 'attached', in balāga, and to take na chudha as 'not pure'. That sets being and nonbeing against the purity of 4a instead of extending it. The Tibetan comment, however, follows Munidatta: 'not even as much as a hair's tip is impure' (skra'i rtse mo tsam yang ma dag pa med pa).

Munidatta: the fourth verse gives the mark of ripened [virtue]{kusala}. The [jewel]{ratna} is the jewel of suchness, endowed with the [ten powers]{dasabala}, the [fearlessnesses]{vaisaradya} and other qualities; pervading the ten directions, it has been 'taken' (hāritam) by us through the force of repeated experience, and by its power the lord-elephant of [ignorance]{avidya} is to be tamed through non-attachment.

Haria, 'having seized, taken' (Sanskrit hṛta); Munidatta paraphrases with hāritam, 'taken'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'phro, 'radiates, spreads out' ('stobs bcu'i rin chen phyogs bcu rnams su 'phro', 'the jewel of the ten powers radiates into the ten directions'), and its comment likewise speaks of radiating ('phro ba).

The Bengali reads vidyākari, 'the elephant of knowledge', and the Tibetan song agrees (rig pa'i glang dbang, 'lord-elephant of knowledge'). Munidatta reads avidyākarīndra, 'the lord-elephant of ignorance', and the Tibetan comment follows him (ma rig pa'i glang po che'i dbang po). I translate the Bengali. The manuscript's word could have lost an initial a-; on the other hand, in his comment on the refrain Munidatta calls Kāṇha himself 'the lord of elephants that is knowledge' (jñānagajendra).

Akilesem̐ is Sanskrit akleśena, in ordinary use 'without trouble, easily', literally 'without affliction'; I keep 'without affliction' to hold both. Munidatta paraphrases 'through non-attachment' (anāsaṅgena). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nyon mongs nyid kyis, 'by the afflictions themselves', without the negative, and its verb btsal, 'sought', may be a slip for btul, 'tamed' (a guess). Damakum̐ looks like a first-person present, 'I tame'; Munidatta's damanaṃ kuru takes it as an imperative. Shastri's text of the comment has 'damanaṃ (madanaṃ)', and the Tibetan comment's myos pa, 'intoxication', agrees with madanaṃ.

proposals.definition: Knowledge (vidyā): in Buddhist thought the opposite of ignorance (avidyā); in the tantras the word can also name a spell and the yogin's female partner. In song 9 the poet tames 'the elephant of knowledge' (vidyākari); Munidatta reads 'the lord-elephant of ignorance' (cp.09.m5), while the Tibetan song has rig pa'i glang dbang.
proposals.rationale: The key word of song 9's last line, where the manuscript (vidyā) and the Tibetan song (rig pa) differ from Munidatta (avidyā). An entry fixes the rendering and keeps it apart from 'ignorance' (avidya). The regular expression stops the form from matching inside অবিদ্যা.

questions: Heading: I added '· Kāṇha' from the attribution kāhnupādānām written before the song (removed from 1a), following the brief's heading pattern and the Tibetan heading. Keep it, drop it, or write 'Kāṇhapāda' to render the -pāda?

1a: I read 'the firm post of evaṃkāra', so the evaṃkāra is (or belongs to) the post that is wrenched. That is close to Munidatta (cp.09.m2). The Tibetan song has 'having made e vaṃ firm, crushes the two pillars'. Which construction do you want? And should bākhoṛa stay singular 'post' when Munidatta and the Tibetan both have a pair of pillars?

4b: chudha is unsettled. I followed Munidatta ('not a hair's tip is impure', cp.09.m4). Reading chudha as śuddha gives the opposite ('not a hair's tip is pure'), and the Tibetan song has 'attachment to things and non-things is impure'. Please decide.

5b: I translated the manuscript's vidyākari as 'the elephant of knowledge', with the Tibetan song, though Munidatta and the Tibetan comment read avidyā, 'the elephant of ignorance' (cp.09.m5). Keep the manuscript, or emend to avidyā?

5b: for akilesem̐, 'without affliction' (marked as the glossary term) or the idiomatic 'easily, without trouble'? And damakum̐ as 'I tame' (first person), or as an imperative, 'tame', the way Munidatta takes it?
2b: is 'and is at peace' (nibitā as nirvṛta) acceptable, given the Tibetan 'became without mind' and Munidatta's 'free of concepts'?
3a–3b: 'the more ... the more' for jima jima ... tima tima, or 'just as ... so', matching Munidatta's simile? And is 'rains down his cheeks' (gala as 'cheek', with the Tibetan) acceptable?
Proposal: a new entry 'vidya' (knowledge), kept distinct from 'avidya' (ignorance). Approve, or fold the word into another entry?
